# TypeScript — Kimox Studio conventions

Extracted from every TypeScript repo in the studio. Where they agree it is a
rule; where they split it is marked and left open.

## Strictness

`strict: true` in every app and package **except the two NestJS APIs**:

| | |
|---|---|
| `mymedesp/apps/api` | partial — `strictNullChecks` + `noImplicitAny`, no `strict` |
| `characters-vault/apps/api` | `strictNullChecks: false`, `noImplicitAny: false` |

That is a gap, not a licence. New code in those APIs is written as if strict
were on: no implicit `any`, and a nullable value is narrowed before use.
Turning the flag on is a migration — see `kx-standards`.

**Packages that others consume are stricter than apps.** `kimox-fw` and
`mymedesp/packages/contracts` both add `noUncheckedIndexedAccess`; `kimox-fw`
also adds `exactOptionalPropertyTypes`. A published or workspace-shared package
takes those flags. An app does not have to.

The reasoning holds: an app owns its callers, a package does not.

## Type placement

Types live next to the code that uses them. No global `types/` directory
anywhere in the studio.

The exception is a cross-boundary contract. `mymedesp/packages/contracts` and
`characters-vault/packages/contracts` hold the types an API and its clients
share, consumed as a workspace package.

Types generated by a tool — Supabase's `Supabase.types.ts` — are committed and
never hand-edited.

**Known drift:** `characters-vault` has a contracts package and still defines
`CharacterResponse` separately in both its API and its webapp. Two definitions
of one wire format is the thing contracts packages exist to prevent.

## `type` or `interface`

`type` for unions, discriminated unions, function signatures, and anything
inferred (`z.infer<typeof schema>`). `interface` for a structural contract
something implements, and for props meant to be extended.

Roughly 60/40 in favour of `type` across the studio. Either is fine where both
would work; do not rewrite one into the other as a drive-by.

## Errors

**No `Result<T, E>` type anywhere.** Do not introduce one.

What is used instead, by context:

- **Domain layer (NestJS):** throw a typed error class — `DomainError`,
  `InfrastructureError`.
- **Route handlers:** return the response, do not throw. `rachafit` returns
  `{ error: { code, message } }` with `code` a string-literal union.
- **Lookups:** `Promise<T | null>` for "not found". Null means absent, not
  failed.

**No non-null assertions (`!`)** in any repo. Narrow with optional chaining,
`??`, or a type predicate (`isPersisted(): this is Ingredient & { id: string }`).

## `as unknown as T` is forbidden

It turns off the checker for that expression and every field read from it.
`mymedesp` uses it routinely — `Ingredient.ts` among others — and nothing else
in the studio does.

Fix the source type, or narrow with a type predicate. If neither is possible
inside the phase's scope, say so in the report rather than casting through
`unknown` and moving on. A single `as T` between two types that genuinely
overlap is a different thing and is fine.

## Imports

- Path alias `@/*` from the repo root, in every project.
- Barrel `index.ts` files define a package's public surface. Inside a package,
  import from the file, not the barrel.
- `import 'server-only'` at the top of any module that must never reach the
  client bundle.

## Named exports only

`export default` is avoided wherever possible — use named exports.

The reason is greppability: an import site invents whatever name it likes for
a default, so a symbol search finds nothing and two callers of one module can
call it two different things. A named export has one name everywhere.

Where a tool requires the default — Next.js pages, layouts and route files —
it stays. Everything else is named.

## Naming

- Components: PascalCase files — `Button.tsx`, `ActivityPicker.tsx`
- Directories: kebab-case — `use-cases/`, `complementary-ingredient/`
- Types and classes: PascalCase
- Generics: `T`, `P`, or a name when there is more than one

## Enums are fine

`enum` where an enum reads better, a string-literal union where that does.
Four repos use unions only and two use real enums; both are accepted, so
follow whatever the file around you already does and do not convert one into
the other as a drive-by.

## Biome, everywhere

Biome is the linter and formatter. `kimox-fw` and
`characters-vault/apps/webapp` already use it; everything else is on ESLint and
Prettier and is expected to migrate.

Swapping linters is a migration — see `kx-standards`. Until a repo has
migrated, run whatever it has. Do not add ESLint config to a
repo already on Biome.

## Unsettled — say which the project uses

**Type-only imports.** `import type { … }` is consistent in `rachafit`,
`kimoxstudio.com`, `alea` and `kimox-fw`. `mymedesp` mostly does not bother.
